newsitem.title: USA: Talkshow murder trial opens in Michigan.
newsitem.headline: Talkshow murder trial opens in Michigan.

text.p: The murder trial of a man who appeared on a daytime talk show, where a gay male admirer revealed that he fantasized about filling the defendant's shorts with whipped cream, opened on Monday.

Oakland County prosecutors have charged Jonathan Schmitz, 26, with first degree murder for shooting Scott Amedure, 32, to death with a shotgun in Amedure's mobile home on March 9, 1995. Three days before the killing, both men appeared on a taped segment of the Jenny Jones syndicated show featuring secret admirers and their fantasies.
Fred Gibson, one of the defence lawyers, argued that Schmitz, 26, was not guilty of first-degree murder because he suffers from mental illnesses and was tricked by the syndicated talk show.

Gibson said the "Jenny Jones" show first lied to Schmitz that his secret admirer could be a woman and then humiliated him when that person turned out to be a man who fantasized about filling Schmitz's shorts with whipped cream.
Schmitz, of Lake Orion, Michigan, and Amedure, of Orion Township, Michigan, appeared on a taping of the show on March 6, 1995. The tape never aired.
Amedure, who was gay and had met Schmitz through a mutual friend, was killed three days later when Schmitz, who says he is not gay, fired two shotgun blasts into his chest, police say.

Oakland County Assistant Prosecutor Roman Kalytiak told the jury in Oakland County Circuit Court that Schmitz was in control of his actions when he bought a shotgun the morning of March 9, 1995, and drove to Amedure's mobile home.
He added that the physical symptoms of Graves disease, which Schmitz says affected his emotions at the time of the crime, arose after the killing.
But Gibson described Schmitz as a troubled young man who moved 14 times in his first 17 years, was suicidal, suffered from manic depression and battled alcohol problems.
"Jonathan, you will hear, went into this believing people were telling him the truth," Gibson said.
After opening remarks, Oakland County Sheriff Detective Craig Stout testified that Schmitz appeared serious and polite during a confession about one hour after the killing.
Schmitz told how, after finding a suggestive note at his apartment he assumed was from Amedure, he withdrew $350 from the bank and purchased shells and a 12-gauge Mossberg shotgun, Stout said.

Schmitz drove to Amedure's home and confronted him about the note. He then walked out of the house and returned with the gun. According to Stout, Amedure screamed "What are you doing?" and held up a wicker chair.

Schmitz fired once from the hip, hitting Amedure in the chest, Stout said, and then fired once more at Amedure on the ground. Schmitz then drove to an Amoco station, called 911, and waited for police to come.

Cross examination of Stout will resume on Tuesday. The jury will have the option of convicting Schmitz of first- or second- degree murder, manslaughter, or reckless discharge causing death. The first-degree murder charge carries a penalty of life without possibility of parole.
